replace.find:
Green tiles. Three rooms to two. Crack across the ceiling north to south. Balcony rail painted twice. Kitchen window that sticks.

She had copied the measurements onto her own pad yesterday. She took out a pencil and began to sketch, not for the customer, just to settle the shape in her hands. A rectangle for the sitting room. A smaller square for the bedroom. The kitchen a narrow strip along the back. She drew the door, the windows, the table position.

Her pencil stopped.

She put her ruler against the sitting room wall and marked the table. Two chairs on the long side. One at the head. One at the foot, facing the door. She drew the fourth stool because Mrs. Wen had written it in. Folding stool, cloth seat worn at the front.

Minyue looked at the sketch. Then she turned the pad sideways and drew the crack, a quick jagged line from the top margin down.

The proportions were wrong for a paper house. Paper houses were usually wider, to make a good show when burned. This one was narrow and long, with the kitchen pinched in. She frowned and flipped to a clean page and measured again from the order slips, thinking she had misread a number.

Seven paces sitting room. Four paces bedroom. She converted to centimeters for the scale model, her pencil moving in short ticks.

It came out the same. Narrow. Long. Kitchen pinched.

She stood up and walked to the shop doorway and looked out at Wenming Road, then back at her sketch. She could see her own building from here, three doors down, the grey arcade pillars and the laundry strung above. Room 302 was on the far side. You could not see the windows from the street.

She sat down again. She drew the ceiling crack once more, slower this time, following the exact kink where it jogged left around the light fitting. In her flat the crack did that. It went north to south and jogged left.

Her hand was shaking. She put the pencil down and pressed her palms flat on the bench. Glue had dried in a thin skin on the wood. It pulled at her skin when she lifted her hands.

“Master,” she said. “Look.”

Hu came over wiping his saw on his trousers. He peered through his thick glasses at her sketch, then at Mrs. Wen’s slips.

“Scale is small,” he said.

“It is my flat,” Minyue said. “Down to the crack. I live there. The kitchen window sticks in the same place. The balcony rail, somebody painted it twice, you can see the drip underneath. Even the table. Even the—”

Hu put his hand over her sketch. His fingers were spotted with glue and ink. The bamboo fan hung from his belt and clicked against the bench.

“Draw for work,” he said. “Not for worry.”

“This is not work, this is—” She stopped. The opera singer hit a high note and held it. “She has never been inside. I never told her the layout.”

“She asked for true,” Hu said. “We build true.”

He returned to his bamboo. The saw started again, a dry rhythmic sound. Minyue stared at her sketch until the lines doubled. She tore the page out, folded it small, and put it in her pocket. Her heart was beating in her throat in a way that made swallowing hard.
replace.with:
Green tiles, one loose, a hollow beneath. Balcony rail painted twice. Kitchen window that sticks. Folding stool, wooden, seat worn at the front.

She did not sketch the flat again. There was no need. The slips only told her what she stepped around every morning: the old drip of paint under the balcony rail, the kitchen window that jammed a finger’s width from the top. Mrs. Wen was no longer describing a flat. She was describing Minyue’s mornings.

“Master,” Minyue said. “The kitchen window sticks. The rail has a drip. She has never been inside.”

Hu did not look up from his bamboo. “She asked for true,” he said. “We build true. Draw for work, not for worry.”

The saw went on, a dry rhythmic sound. Minyue stacked the slips and pressed her palms flat on the bench. Glue had dried in a thin skin on the wood. It pulled at her skin when she lifted her hands.
